provenance: Researched dossier with an explicitly reviewed identity match. Dates may follow a stated scholarly convention; source boundaries are independently attributed.
summary: The Roman state centered on Constantinople, whose inhabitants called themselves Romans; its language, territory and institutions changed across more than a millennium.
currency: Gold solidus in the early Byzantine period; coinage changed substantially over later centuries.
rulers: Selected rulers: Constantine I, 306–337; Justinian I, 527–565.
economy: Constantinople occupied a major intersection of east–west trade; taxes and army payments used imperial coinage.
military: Justinian recovered western territories, but subsequent Persian, Arab, Latin and Turkish advances reduced imperial control.
contributions: Preserved and transformed Roman law, Greek learning, Christian architecture, mosaics and manuscript traditions.
origin: Constantine inaugurated Constantinople in 330; eastern Roman institutions continued through the collapse of western imperial government.
decline: The Fourth Crusade fractured the empire in 1204; after restoration, a diminished state ended with the Ottoman capture of Constantinople in 1453.
periodNote: 330 is a conventional starting point, not a declaration of a new Byzantine state. The Latin occupation interrupted Constantinople-based rule in 1204–1261.
name: Byzantine Empire
identityNote: Same continuing eastern Roman polity. The dossier begins at Constantinople’s foundation in 330; AtlasPI begins at the imperial division in 395. Preserve this start-date convention explicitly; do not attach to the city Constantinople or the Ghassanid Kingdom.
